rv.q: She’s utterly, mesmerisingly convincing as she inhabits Holiday, quipping with deceptive lightness that Philly is the only place that put her in jail.
It seems almost redundant to report that McDonald gives a powerhouse performance as an ailing but still proud Billie Holiday.
When McDonald warbles as Lady Day, it’s as if she’s pouring divine nectar into your ears.
Her performance works from the inside out.
Vocally, it's astonishing: McDonald gets the slur and mischievous yelp in Holiday's voice.
Lanie Robertson wrote this astonishing play after a boyfriend told him that he had seen Billie Holiday in 1959 in 'a little dive' in north Philadelphia.
But, while McDonald is a supreme artist who captures the style and spirit of Holiday, there is something morbid about the show’s fascination with the singer’s decline and fall.
It's a performance of immense technical skill, if at times one that feels slightly mechanical and uncanny, and it propels a production that can feel formulaic and even a little ghoulish.
It is hard to praise highly enough her brilliant act of recreation. But a little stage drunkenness goes a long way, and 95 minutes of it is more than sufficient.
In fact, impersonation isn't quite right; this is more like a transfixing act of total transformation.
Triumphant yet tragic, this is a breathtaking theatrical experience.
No wait is too long for acting of this calibre, which transcends ready-made definitions of impersonation to suggest a spiritual alignment...
One American great inhabits another in this superior cabaret, as the Broadway legend Audra McDonald slips into the skin - and unforgettable voice - of jazz icon Billie Holiday.
This is as close as you’re going to get to hearing that sad, smoky, heaven-tinged sound for real.
It may not be a great play but it is an astonishing performance.
McDonald doesn't imitate Holliday, she recreates her and makes the songs her own while still keeping them Lady Day's.

An astonishing portrayal of one of America’s finest female jazz singers, McDonald eases herself into character, leaving us with beautifully sentimental renditions of some of Billie Holiday’s classics.

cn.t: McDonald delivers a technically brilliant, emotionally resonant portrayal of Billie Holiday that transcends mere impersonation, though some find Robertson's play uncomfortably focused on the jazz legend's tragic final decline.
